what: matched-load incline: center of mass, friction and first instability. One motor slowly tilts a shared deck beneath two freestanding towers. The green and orange towers have the same base, external frame, 22-part inventory and 46.46 g catalogue mass. The eight red ballast plates sit low inside the green tower and high inside the orange tower. Neither tower is fastened to the deck. Compare each tower's first instability while it is still clear of the tall yellow catch wall: does its base move downhill while it stays upright, or does it lean away from the deck normal? The wall arrests later motion. The supplied comparison exchanges only the ballast heights between the lanes. One motor tilts two equally heavy free towers with low or high internal ballast. In the native recordings, high ballast tips near 15° and low ballast slides near 22°. Swap the ballast heights between lanes; a tall passive wall arrests the later motion.
try: Reset the complete scene, load this model’s example program and run it. Reset again before every repeat or comparison.
Before the deck moves, predict which tower should slide first and which should tip first. Look for the red ballast: color identifies a lane, while ballast height is the quantity being changed.

Watch the first sustained motion of each tower from the side. Sliding means the bottom of the base travels along the deck while the tower remains nearly perpendicular to it. Tipping means the tower rotates relative to the deck. A tower's top moving sideways is not enough to distinguish these events.

Record the actual deck inclination at the first clear slide or tip, before that load reaches the yellow wall. Judge the deck against horizontal and each tower against the deck. Small contact movements are different from a sustained event. A later lean against the wall is not the tipping threshold; a load that slides first may rotate later.

The program requests +23.5 degrees at 1 degree per second, briefly holds, then returns the deck at 3 degrees per second and holds at zero. Watch the free loads throughout. The passive wall is there to arrest later movement; it does not stand either load upright or restore its starting place.

Predict what should happen after the ballast-height swap. Import the complete tipline-swapped.ldr model afresh and run the same tipline.bw program. The green tower now has high ballast and the orange tower low ballast; their bases, outer frames, parts and total masses are unchanged.

Compare the first events across both runs. Does behavior follow ballast height when its lane changes? Reload the complete saved model before each repeat. Returning motor A to its starting angle restores the deck, but it does not stand up a fallen tower or replace a tower that has slid.
why: A tower can lose stability in two different ways. It can slide when the downhill component of gravity exceeds the friction available at its base. It can tip when gravity's line of action reaches the downhill edge of the supported base. Raising the same ballast raises the center of mass without changing total mass or base width, so a smaller deck angle can carry that line of action beyond the edge. The friction reference stays the same when the contact materials stay the same. Moving ballast also changes rotational inertia; using a slow tilt helps make the static comparison useful, while the actual motion still has to be observed.
matters: Objects with the same weight and outside dimensions can have different stability because their mass is distributed differently. In the two supplied native recordings of the 174-part model, the main model's high orange tower first tipped at 14.97909 degrees and its low green tower first slid at 22.13048 degrees. After the ballast-height swap, the high green tower tipped at 14.98017 degrees and the low orange tower slid at 22.12919 degrees. Both native runs and the paired comparison passed their declared checks. The outcome follows ballast height rather than lane or color. These are simulator observations of the exported files, not a browser-integration check or a physical build.
question: After the same ballast plates are moved from low to high inside the green tower and from high to low inside the orange tower, which first-motion behaviors should exchange lanes, and why?
answer: The high-ballast configuration should tip first, while the low-ballast configuration should slide first; those behaviors should follow the ballast when it changes lanes. The supplied native recordings show that exchange: tipping occurs near 15 degrees and sliding near 22 degrees in both lanes. A high center of mass brings the gravity line to the base edge below the frictional sliding reference. With low ballast, the calculated tipping reference is above the sliding reference, allowing the base to move while the tower is still upright. Equal total mass does not imply equal tipping stability. The yellow wall acts later; leaning against it is not the measured first tipping event.
further: The common downhill base half-width is 16 mm. Actual prepared center-of-mass heights are approximately 32.3 mm with low ballast and 61.6 mm with high ballast. A sharp-edge static calculation gives tipping references near 26.35 and 14.56 degrees. The native base corner radius is 0.4 mm; the corresponding rounded-edge references are approximately 26.06 and 14.30 degrees. These are calculated references, separate from the recorded event angles.

The prepared native body-pair friction coefficient is 0.4, giving an ideal sliding reference of about 21.80 degrees. The observer identifies tipping as at least 5 degrees of downhill lean relative to the deck, and sliding as at least 2 mm of downhill base travel while relative tilt is below 3 degrees. Each event must persist for 0.10 seconds. These visible-motion criteria, finite tilt speed and rounded contacts shift a detected event from a static threshold.

The low tower's calculated tipping reference assumes that its base is still sticking. Once the base is sliding, its acceleration and contact-force balance have changed. The calculation does not say that an already sliding tower must tip when the deck passes that angle.

Would simply multiplying all masses by the same factor change either ideal static threshold if the center of mass, base and friction coefficient stayed unchanged? The mass factor cancels from both balances. Moving ballast changes the center of mass, so it is a different experiment.

Compare Tilt Lab, where deck inclination directs a rolling marble, and the clutch load bench, where limited friction permits relative rotation. Tipline compares sliding contact with overturning of an entirely free supported load.

Use the supplied finite program for the comparison. Manual control has not been qualified. Requested motor angles are not physical stops, and the encoder is not a direct measurement of either free tower. Reload the entire saved model after an interruption or manual movement. Browser integration and a physical build require their own checks.

The catch wall remains clear through the initial useful motion. The high configurations reached more than 26.7 degrees of lean with over 10.2 mm clearance; the low configurations traveled more than 10.3 mm upright with over 41.5 mm clearance. Later wall contact is approximate in the simulator: the largest recorded nominal wall-face overlap was about 1.81 mm. Judge the first instability before this contact, not the final leaned pose.
formula: Sharp-edge static tipping: theta_tip = atan(b/h), where b is the downhill support half-width and h the center-of-mass height. For the native rounded base reference, theta_tip,r = atan((b-r)/(h-r)). Coulomb sliding: theta_slide = atan(mu). Here b = 16 mm, r = 0.4 mm, h_low approximately 32.3 mm, h_high approximately 61.6 mm, and prepared mu = 0.4. Rounded tipping references are approximately 26.06 degrees (low) and 14.30 degrees (high); sliding is approximately 21.80 degrees. The smaller static reference predicts the first instability. Recorded onset uses the stated displacement/tilt and persistence criteria; these formulas do not prescribe a trajectory.
